title: Continuous Hasenbusch transport towards gauge diffusion with fermions
abstract: Incorporating dynamical fermions is a central challenge for diffusion samplers of lattice gauge theories. We propose an analytic pseudofermion sampler based on continuous Hasenbusch transport as a component for gauge diffusion. The construction uses shifted linear solves and a finite-path correction, requiring neither explicit fermion determinant evaluation nor a learned pseudofermion model. We demonstrate the coupling in the two-flavour Schwinger model without neural networks, obtaining corrected physical observables compatible with independent references. We also show why accurate covariance transport can leave large weight fluctuations, tracing them to the backward transition density. This analysis leads to a correction based on the Wilson operator trace that reduces log-weight variance without changing the generated fields or increasing the number of Dirac operator applications. The predicted improvement is verified on previously unused gauge backgrounds. These results provide an analytic option for incorporating fermions in gauge diffusion and a guide to controlling its correction weights.
summary: This paper introduces an analytic method to incorporate dynamical fermions into lattice gauge theory simulations using continuous Hasenbusch transport. By developing a pseudofermion sampler that avoids complex determinant calculations, the authors significantly reduce weight fluctuations in the Monte Carlo sampling process. This provides a robust, analytic tool for simulating fermionic systems in lattice field theory.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is incorporating dynamical fermions into lattice gauge theory sampling, specifically within gauge diffusion samplers.
main_result: The authors propose and demonstrate an analytic pseudofermion sampler using continuous Hasenbusch transport that yields corrected physical observables compatible with independent references.
method: The method involves constructing an analytic pseudofermion sampler based on continuous Hasenbusch transport, utilizing shifted linear solves and a finite-path correction to avoid explicit fermion determinant evaluation.
model_or_system: The work is tested in the two-flavour Schwinger model on a lattice, involving gauge fields and pseudofermion fields governed by the Wilson operator.
key_observables: Physical observables (e.g., mean plaquette, fermion condensate), and diagnostics include log-weight variance ($	ext{Var}(\log W)$) and the ratio of log-weight variances ($	ext{BS}/	ext{B}$).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the bare fermion mass ($m$), the gauge coupling ($ eta$), and the number of diffusion steps ($K$).
main_assumptions: The approach relies on an analytic construction, explicitly avoiding the use of neural networks, and the analysis is performed on finite-volume lattices.
figures_summary: Figures compare log-weight variance and $	ext{BS}/	ext{B}$ ratios across different step counts ($K=64, 256$) and demonstrate the predicted reduction in variance on unused gauge backgrounds.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of fermion sampling, details the continuous Hasenbusch transport formalism, presents the analytic correction derived from the Wilson operator trace, and validates the resulting improved path estimator on test backgrounds.
why_interesting: While focused on lattice gauge theory, the core techniques—developing analytically controlled estimators for complex path integrals and reducing weight fluctuations in Monte Carlo sampling—are highly relevant to simulating quantum many-body systems where exact sampling is intractable.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Differences from the corresponding independent references, in units of the fixed precision tolerance. Bars show individual 95% jackknife intervals; the shaded band is the target interval. The diffusion-only study uses 8000 paths and a 32,000-field reference; the mixture uses 32,000 paths and a 64,000-field reference. All six mixture intervals also meet the stronger simultaneous criterion described in section 5.1.

Figure 2. Observable variance multiplied by sample count, relative to the diffusion component alone. The controls use the diffusion density qD and pure-gauge density qQ, respectively. All components use BS at K = 256. The mixture has 32,000 fields, and each component control has 16,000; they share samples and are not independent replications. Bars show point estimates without confidence intervals.

Figure 3. Finite-step predictions and measurements on previously unused backgrounds. A denotes independent-refresh AIS; numerical suffixes give the number of pseudofermion steps. Left: log- weight variance for 96 method conditions. Right: paired BS/B variance ratios for K = 64 and 256. Error bars show one standard error from a 16-block jackknife of 256 pseudofermion samples per condition. The spectra and predictions were fixed before generating these samples.
